skills.name: Business units and the sole proprietor

note.text: A business unit organises resources to supply goods or services. A sole proprietorship has one owner, although it may employ workers. In the ordinary unincorporated model, the owner bears business losses and personal liability can extend beyond the funds invested. Direct control can make decisions quick, while limited finance and dependence on one person can constrain the business. Revenue is sales income; profit is revenue less the relevant costs. Neither one owner nor a small size guarantees profit.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain sole ownership, distinguish revenue from profit and identify an ownership trade-off. Builds on: Form Three’s production, resources and choice. Leads to: partnerships, which share ownership, resources and decisions.

sections.heading: Understand the economics
sections.text: A business unit organises resources to supply goods or services. A sole proprietorship has one owner, although it may employ workers. In the ordinary unincorporated model, the owner bears business losses and personal liability can extend beyond the funds invested. Direct control can make decisions quick, while limited finance and dependence on one person can constrain the business. Revenue is sales income; profit is revenue less the relevant costs. Neither one owner nor a small size guarantees profit.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: Bih owns a fictional Buea repair stall and hires an assistant. The assistant’s wage does not make the assistant a co-owner. Bih chooses services and keeps the accounting profit after costs, but also bears losses. The example illustrates ownership, not a claim that any activity may operate without local formalities.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Ask who owns, who decides and who bears loss. Separate employees from owners. Calculate profit from comparable-period revenue and costs, not from money in the till alone. Do not treat the school model as a set of registration or tax instructions.

key_words.meaning: ownership by one person, even when employees are hired
personal responsibility that can extend beyond the owner’s business investment in the ordinary model
the owner’s ability to make decisions without co-owner approval
sales revenue less the relevant recorded costs for the period

mistake.wrong: Hiring a worker automatically creates shared ownership.
mistake.right: sole ownership: ownership by one person, even when employees are hired.
mistake.why: A wage contract is different from owning a stake in the business.

steps: Use the same period and currency.

cards.idea: Distinguish these features before judging a business.
example: sole ownership: ownership by one person, even when employees are hired.
unlimited liability: personal responsibility that can extend beyond the owner’s business investment in the ordinary model.
direct control: the owner’s ability to make decisions without co-owner approval.
accounting profit: sales revenue less the relevant recorded costs for the period.

cards.idea: Use the stated case evidence to identify the economic feature.
example: Bih alone owns the stall while an assistant earns a wage.
An unpaid business debt may expose the proprietor’s personal assets.
Bih changes the service list without consulting a partner.
The stall deducts its costs from its sales revenue.

cards.idea: Explain a consequence instead of assuming every option has the same effect.
example: sole ownership: A wage contract is different from owning a stake in the business.
unlimited liability: The ordinary model does not separate the proprietor’s liability as a limited company does.
direct control: Quick decisions remain exposed to mistakes and limited expertise.
accounting profit: Costs must be deducted before interpreting the remainder as profit.

questions.prompt: An invented Buea stall receives {revenue} CFA francs in sales and incurs {cost} CFA francs in the stated period. Calculate its accounting profit, ignoring taxes and other adjustments.

misconceptions.explain: Sales revenue has not yet had costs deducted.
Costs reduce the remainder; do not add them to revenue.

solution: Profit is revenue minus the stated costs.
